name: Saanich
confidence_why: Montler 1986, the reference grammar, treats Saanich stress as a competition between lexically specified root and suffix classes, while Leonard 2007 argues that most disyllabic roots and root-plus-lexical-suffix stems follow a right-aligned trochee that prefers full vowels over schwa; Leonard still grants a lexically stressed residue and Montler 2025 still calls stress not fully predictable, with certain suffixes pulling it off the stem, so the morphological coding stands over a weight-based default.

sweep_summary: Only one works with stress in the title: Leonard 2006, 'Formalising stress in SENĆOŦEN' (UVic MA thesis, 108 pp), already in our bibliography. The thesis PDF could not be obtained (UVicSpace hdl 1828/2105 could not be reached by automated download on every endpoint; the 2019 Internet Archive copy is unreachable;4 (held by the project from the 2026-09-16 check), was read in full. Both argue that stress in SENĆOŦEN lexical stems is largely phonological — right-aligned trochaic (penultimate tendency) with weight sensitivity (full vowel over schwa) — and that much of Montler 1986's morpho-lexical root/suffix hierarchy is unnecessary, while conceding a residue of unpredictable cases and a scope limited to disyllabic roots and lexical-suffix stems. This refines rather than overturns the catalog's 'morphological' coding, which rests on Montler 1986 (the reference grammar by the principal field linguist) and is still echoed by Montler's 2025 online grammar ('stress is not completely predictable'; held by the project). Recommend keeping Montler 1986 as deciding source and adding a note that Leonard 2006/2007 reanalyses most lexical-stem stress as a weight-sensitive right-aligned trochee with residual lexical exceptions. new_statements.quote: In this paper, I support both Montler (1986:23) and Kiyota (2003:7) in their first claim, that stress tends to be penultimate. However, my research does not support their second claim, that stress in SENĆOŦEN is a morphologically complex system. Instead, I argue that the stress pattern of many SENĆOŦEN lexical stems can be accounted for by assuming that left-headed binary feet are aligned to the right edge of a lexical stem and that SENĆOŦEN is sensitive to the phonological weight distinction between full vowel and schwa.

new_statements.reading: Leonard reanalyses the SENĆOŦEN stress pattern that Montler 1986 describes as a morpho-lexical hierarchy (strong/weak/vowelless roots vs strong/ambivalent/weak/unstressed suffixes) as mostly phonological: a right-aligned trochee (penultimate default) overridden by weight, full vowel > schwa. She restricts the claim to disyllabic roots and root+lexical-suffix stems, explicitly leaves a residue of unpredictable, lexically specified cases (p. 30; fn 18; ex. 7b), and calls the account preliminary. This is the only dedicated stress study of the language and it is first-hand (fieldwork plus Montler's published data).

new_statements.quote: The stress system of the Salish languages has been traditionally thought of as being highly morpho-lexical. Montler (1986: 23) states that in SENCOTEN, roots and affixes are lexically specified for their stress properties. [...] However, in this thesis, I show that there is much less morpho-lexical stress in SENCOTEN than previously thought. [...] I show that it is the weight distinction between full vowels and schwa that determines where stress will be assigned. In addition, I am able to show that metrical feet are grouped into trochees and that these trochaic feet are aligned to the right edge of the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is assigned by vowel weight (full vowel outranks schwa) within right-aligned trochaic feet, i.e. a penultimate default overridden by weight; the morpho-lexical root/affix hierarchy of Montler 1986 is largely unnecessary.

new_statements.identity_note: All three works describe the Saanich (SENĆOŦEN, W̱SÁNEĆ) dialect of Northern Straits Salish specifically, not Songish, Lummi, Samish or Sooke; Leonard's abstract calls it 'SENCOTEN (a dialect of North Straits Salish)'. new_statements.quote: In general, if there is one A, Á, I, O, or U in the word, that one is the stressed vowel. [...] If the word has only E vowels, it is often a good guess to stress the second E from the end. [...] But sometimes your guess will be wrong, because stress is not completely predictable in SENĆOŦEN. The word EWENE ‘nothing,’ for example, has three E vowels, but in this word, it is the first E that is stressed. Sometimes a word has more than one A, Á, I, O, or U. In such cases, it is usually the last A, Á, I, O, or U that takes the stress. But these are just rules of thumb and not one hundred percent reliable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same weight-driven picture as the existing Leonard 2007 statement (full vowel > schwa, penultimate default among schwas, lexical residue); adds the 'last full vowel wins when there are several' rule of thumb. Notably Montler's own 2025 grammar states the pattern in weight terms rather than the 1986 morpheme-valence hierarchy. Pedagogical register, no formal analysis.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A full vowel (A, Á, I, O, U) attracts stress over schwa (E); with several full vowels it is usually the last one; in all-schwa words the penultimate schwa is the default; these are rules of thumb and stress is not fully predictable (e.g. EWENE 'nothing' stresses the first E). Point 6 also says stressed vowels are louder, longer and stronger. §34 keeps Montler's strong/weak/zero stems but frames them as vowel-shift (metathesis) behaviour under suffixation and notes zero stems have no stressed vowel of their own so stress goes to the suffix vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: EWENE 'nothing' (first of three schwas stressed); 'rules of thumb and not one hundred percent reliable'; §34 point 10: for some younger L1 speakers the weak/strong stem distinction (vowel shift) is variable. new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per full word, on the root or a suffix (never a prefix), decided by lexically specified stress valences: roots are strong, weak or vowelless; suffixes strong, ambivalent, weak or unstressed; the stronger morpheme wins, with a penultimate tendency as tiebreaker (equal-valence suffixes or two-vowel suffixes take penultimate stress, §1.4.3: 'Given a form with a number of suffixes of equal valence, stress will fall on the penultimate vowel'). Penultimate placement can trigger metathesis of a strong root's non-schwa vowel with the following obstruent. Unstressed vowels reduce to schwa (§1.5.4).
new_statements.secondary_stress: §1.4: 'Three levels with respect to stress can be recognized: primary (V́), secondary (V ‘), and unstressed (V). There is one primary stressed vowel per full word [..]. Any non-schwa vowel and some schmas that do not carry primary stress carry secondary stress.' (sic: 'schwas'); words with more than one non-schwa are uncommon, /i/ from vocalised /y/ the usual case.
new_statements.exceptions: Two-vowel suffixes with differing valences (/-əláʔ/ stressed on 2nd vowel; =aθin stressed on whichever vowel is penultimate); vowelless roots with a resonant C2 strengthened to weak roots before vowel-initial suffixes; weak consonant-initial suffixes (-naxʷ) stressed only after vowelless roots; 'Since stress valence of most roots has not yet been determined, underlying forms will not be prejudiced as to stress valence'; §1.5.4 lists suffixes that resist reduction (-si, -i), suffixes that take stress but leave the root vowel intact (=éw̕txʷ, =iɬč, -naŋət, =sis), loans with unstressed full vowels (lisék, sə́nti, stíqiw) and a few unexplained words (siʔém̕, piʔátəɬ, siʔétən, sx̣ʷiʔém̕).

new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per lexical stem (root, or root + lexical suffix). Default: a single left-headed binary foot (trochee) aligned to the right edge of the stem, i.e. penultimate stress (ALIGN-R >> WSP >> MAX-mu, DEP-mu, HEAD-L >> FT-BIN >> PARSE-sigma, p. 76). Weight override: only full vowels are moraic, schwa is weightless (and featureless), so a full vowel is stressed over a schwa wherever it sits (e.g. sqəléw' 'beaver', final stress); two full vowels or two schwas -> penultimate (sk'ʷáti, qə́ləx̌); unstressed full vowels reduce to schwa; surface [i] from schwa+glide counts as weightless (ti?tás). Prefixes/particles not treated; she argues stress is phonologically predictable for the majority of lexical stems rather than assigned by Montler's morpho-lexical root/suffix hierarchy.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated in the pages read: the analysis builds one right-aligned trochee per stem with PARSE-sigma ranked lowest, so no iterative footing or secondary stress is claimed; no occurrence of 'secondary' in the scanned pages.
new_statements.exceptions: Scope limited to disyllabic roots and root+lexical-suffix stems (transitivity morphology, person markers, reduplication, infixation, stress shift/metathesis, particles and clitics left for future work, pp. 1, 77). Conformity of root+lexical-suffix sets to the pattern 'approximately 70%-90%', the two-schwa suffix set excepted (p. 75). Apparent exceptions explained (4.3, pp. 70-74): antepenultimate stress with a historic middle /-m/ or with stacked lexical suffixes (stress domain = inner 'phonological stem', outer suffix outside it), excrescent schwas that do not count, and a ban on adjacent coronal clusters (nəw̕=ə́qs-t). True exceptions (4.4, pp. 74-75): =iqʷ 'head' always stressed regardless of root vowel, nəs=ə́t 'four times', ɫxʷ=ə́t 'three times' -- 'It may be that these lexical suffixes, or these particular words are in fact lexically specified for stress' (homophony avoidance with durative [ət] suggested for the latter). Apparent iambs tiʔtás, sxʷiʔém' analysed as weightless schwa+glottalised glide in the first syllable (p. 36).
new_statements.identity_note: SENĆOŦEN = Saanich dialect of North(ern) Straits Salish, W̱SÁNEĆ (Saanich) community, southern Vancouver Island; data from the author's 2004-2006 fieldwork with Saanich elders (FN 2004/2006) plus Montler 1986/1991 forms re-checked with elders.

readall_conflicts: One analytical disagreement, already known to the catalog: Montler 1986 (§1.4) treats Saanich stress as morpho-lexical, each root and suffix carrying a lexically specified stress valence (strong/weak/vowelless roots; strong/ambivalent/weak/unstressed suffixes) that competes for the single primary stress, with penultimate stress only as a tendency among morphemes of equal valence. Leonard 2006 (abstract) and Leonard 2007 (the existing statement) reanalyse the same data as phonological: right-aligned trochee (penultimate default) overridden by vowel weight (full vowel > schwa), leaving a residue of unpredictable cases. Montler's own 2025 online grammar (Notes on Pronunciation, point 6) now states the pattern in weight terms, a full vowel takes the stress, the last one if several, the penultimate E in all-schwa words, while still calling these rules of thumb that are not one hundred percent reliable (EWENE 'nothing'). All sources agree on one primary stress per full word, prefixes/particles unstressed, and the penultimate tendency; no source claims fixed or absent stress. sources.quote: Montler (1986: 23) states that in SENCOTEN, roots and affixes are lexically specified for their stress properties. He claims that these roots and affixes are in a hierarchical relationship and compete with each other for stress assignment. However, in this thesis, I show that there is much less morpho-lexical stress in SENCOTEN than previously thought. ... I show that it is the weight distinction between full vowels and schwa that determines where stress will be assigned. In addition, I am able to show that metrical feet are grouped into trochees and that these trochaic feet are aligned to the right edge of the word.

sources.quote: In general, if there is one A, Á, I, O, or U in the word, that one is the stressed vowel. [...] If the word has only E vowels, it is often a good guess to stress the second E from the end. [...] But sometimes your guess will be wrong, because stress is not completely predictable in SENĆOŦEN. The word EWENE ‘nothing,’ for example, has three E vowels, but in this word, it is the first E that is stressed. Sometimes a word has more than one A, Á, I, O, or U. In such cases, it is usually the last A, Á, I, O, or U that takes the stress. But these are just rules of thumb and not one hundred percent reliable.
